name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: CrewAI: A Python Framework for Orchestrating Multi-Agent AI Workflows
answer: CrewAI is an open-source Python framework, made by CrewAI Inc. and released under the MIT licence, for orchestrating role-playing autonomous AI agents that collaborate on complex tasks. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above the language models and tools it calls. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that it pairs role-based crews with a deterministic Flows layer, so the same framework covers quick prototypes and production systems with tracing, guardrails and governance.

sections.body: CrewAI is a framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents, built and maintained by CrewAI Inc. and published under the MIT licence. Its repository, crewAIInc/crewAI, is written in Python and had its most recent push on 3 October 2026, with roughly 59,297 stars at the time of writing. The official site describes it as an open-source framework for building and orchestrating multi-agent AI workflows, where developers define autonomous agents with specific roles, goals and backstories that can use tools, process tasks and interact with each other. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack: it does not train models or serve them itself, it coordinates language models, tools and data sources into multi-step work. The site frames this as collaborative intelligence, agents working together rather than one model answering one prompt.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs CrewAI handles are multi-step, language-heavy automations that need reasoning over unstructured data, tool and API calls, and several collaborating agents, such as research, analysis, drafting and review. The site's own tutorial builds a researcher agent that searches the web with SerperDevTool and produces a report, and its NVIDIA collaboration demo shows agents that automatically write project documentation. The site lists role-based crews with specialists, shared memory and handoffs, plus a production path with tracing, guardrails and an Agent Management Platform. It is strongest where a task decomposes into roles and steps, and the site explicitly recommends it over RPA for cognitive work, while noting enterprises often keep RPA for deterministic UI workflows. It also supports sequential execution and, through Flows, conditional branching and state management.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: CrewAI is a Python framework, so working Python knowledge is the main prerequisite, and the site's tutorial assumes you can install packages, manage an API key in a .env file and read a short script. The core concepts are few and named plainly: an agent has a role, goal and backstory, a task is a unit of work assigned to an agent, a crew is a collection of agents and tasks, and a process defines the execution strategy, with Process.sequential running tasks one after another. No mathematics or systems knowledge beyond ordinary programming is required to start, because the framework calls hosted language models rather than training them. For beginners the official site offers a developer portal, a tutorial that walks through a complete working example, and agent-ready documentation including an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file. The harder learning curve comes later, when moving from a demo to production, where the site's guidance on architecture, token spend and governance becomes relevant.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around CrewAI is visible in the site's own material. There is a crewai-tools package for external tools such as web search, and integrations with model providers including Cerebras and with NVIDIA NIM microservices as part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise, which lets any NVIDIA customer power CrewAI agents and flows with models hosted on NVIDIA. The site links to a GitHub repository with complete example code, a developer portal, an MCP server and llms-full.txt for agent-ready documentation. Community scale is suggested by the repository's roughly 59,297 stars and by the site's claim of 40,000 GitHub stars at the time of the NVIDIA announcement, along with reports drawing on thousands of professionals building AI agents. The site also publishes survey material, including a 2026 State of Agentic AI report based on 500 executives, which shows a market context rather than a support channel.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: CrewAI is presented as serving both ends. A short script with an agent, a task and a crew can be running in minutes, which is the prototyping story the tutorial demonstrates. For production, the site describes Agentic Systems that combine a deterministic backbone called Flows with intelligence deployed where it matters, and it says Flows are a very thin code layer with almost no abstractions, just flexible decorators and state management, handling conditional branching, state across steps and custom business logic with the same inputs producing the same execution path. The production path adds tracing, guardrails and an Agent Management Platform. The cost of this range is that the simple crew abstraction is not enough on its own for production, and the site's own architecture article criticises unbounded agency and prompt chains passing as agents, so teams must learn the Flows layer and accept more structure to get observability, governance and cost control.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site makes strong adoption claims: 1.4 billion agentic automations, 60 percent of the Fortune 500, and production use cases at large enterprises such as PwC and startups such as Parloa, alongside a claim of having watched 1.7 billion agentic workflows run across enterprise customers in healthcare, consumer packaged goods, finance, logistics and professional services. Its 2026 survey reports that 100 percent of surveyed enterprises plan to expand agentic AI use, 81 percent have fully adopted or are actively scaling it, and 57 percent prefer building on existing open-source tools rather than starting from scratch. These figures come from CrewAI's own material and should be read as vendor-published. On that basis CrewAI is a current choice in the agent orchestration category rather than a legacy one, and skills in it map to roles building agentic automation, though the site does not publish salary or hiring data.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: CrewAI is Python-first, and the site positions it as the open, Python-first option for multi-agent crews, in contrast with Microsoft Agent Framework, which targets .NET and Azure ecosystems, and Automation Anywhere, which is an enterprise RPA platform with AI-assisted bots for UI and legacy system automation. The site says buyers typically compare CrewAI, Microsoft Agent Framework and Automation Anywhere, and it also lists AutoGen and MetaGPT in its framework comparison. The polyglot pattern is that CrewAI handles the cognitive, language-heavy orchestration while other systems handle deterministic UI or legacy automation, and many enterprises run both. It calls language models through provider integrations such as Cerebras and NVIDIA, and it uses tools and MCP for external capabilities, so it is normally one layer in a stack rather than the whole stack.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about some weaknesses. It says most agentic implementations are either too rigid or too loose, criticises prompt chains passing as agents and autonomous agents without architectural constraints, and warns that token spend can explode, with a ten-step run reaching 500,000 to 2 million tokens and 60 to 80 percent of enterprise token spend going to use cases that have not proven business value. It also reports data readiness and integration challenges at 35 percent and insufficient talent at 33 percent as top obstacles. What the official material does not settle is benchmarking against rival frameworks, detailed pricing for the Agent Management Platform, and independent verification of the adoption figures, which are vendor-published. The site also does not say how much of the framework's behaviour is stable across versions, so a reader should treat those points as open.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
